# The name Haoma and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Haoma** opens ​onto an entire world: the domain of sacred plant, immortality, a Zoroastrian tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name ‌and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain ‌that makes the whole structure addressable. *haoma* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Haoma
- **ASCII form:** ​haoma
- **Meaning:** "The pressed one"
- **Domain of influence:** Sacred Plant, Immortality
- **Pantheon:** Zoroastrian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀 (Avestan)

## Overview

**Haoma** (*haoma*) — Sacred Plant, Immortality · The pressed one — ​belongs to the Zoroastrian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sacred Plant, Immortality". The name means "The pressed one".

**Haoma** is sacred plant, immortality. The name means "The pressed one" ​and belongs to the zoroastrian tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Haoma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/haoma/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. ​The plain ASCII form *haoma* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

​The name is attested in Avestan as **𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀**. Etymologically it means "The pressed one".

The ASCII form *haoma* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a ‌technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Haoma** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics ​its ASCII form would lose.

- **h** → **H** — Same, capitalized

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Avestan as **𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Haoma*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Haoma is the sacred plant and ‌divinity praised in Yasna 9–10.
- The initial h is the Avestan letter h (𐬵).
- The diphthong ao is written with a (𐬀) followed by o (𐬊).

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the ​name is **/haoma/** — Restored scholarly form.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **haoma** — The canonical restored form Haoma.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "haoma" with the stress and length ‌implied by the scholarly restoration "Haoma".

The ASCII form "haoma" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Haoma" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which ​Haoma was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration Haoma keeps the prosodic information visible even ‌when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

## Mythology

The stories of Haoma place sacred plant, immortality at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Haoma appears in zoroastrian tradition ​as sacred plant, immortality. The name's meaning, "The pressed one", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Haoma in ritual, text, and iconography, ​ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Haoma survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, ​and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Haoma gives the figure a stable name around which ​these variants orbit.

### Haoma Who Was First Pressed (Yašt 9)

The ninth Yašt is the hymn of the plant made god: Haoma, green and with golden eyes, who was first pressed ​on the heights of Hara (Yašt 9.16, 19). The Avesta remembers him as both herb and yazata — the only deity of the Iranian pantheon who is simultaneously the offering itself, pounded ‌fresh on the pestle each night in the Yasna. His first-pressing on Hara Berezaiti, the Alborz, the axis of the world, is the same mountain where Mithra keeps his thousand-eared, thousand-eyed watch ​(Yašt 10.13) — sacrament and covenant share one summit. His color and eyes passed into iconography: the golden-green plant appears on Sasanian silver among the emblems of the consecrated banquet. **Haoma collapses ‌the distance between altar and deity: the offering does not merely represent the god — it is the god, crushed to give life**.

### Zarathustra's Reproach and the Roll of the Righteous (Yasna ​9)

The most human scene in the Avesta opens the ninth chapter of the Yasna. Zarathuštra reproaches the plant: the karpans and the kavis — the sacrificial guilds he condemns — pressed ‌you, Haoma, for the stupefying draught, and the plant stands accused by its own prophet (Yasna 9.1–3). Haoma answers with a catalogue of the righteous who pressed him rightly: Yima, who won ​the sun; Thraētaona, who struck down the three-mouthed Aži Dahāka; Kərəsāspa, who slew the horned dragon Gandarəβa; and Vīštāspa, who first confessed the good religion (Yasna 9.3–8). The exchange is unique — ‌a prophet interrogating his own sacrament — and its verdict is exact: The scene gives the tradition its own charter myth of ritual reform, rare in the ancient world. **the plant is ​holy; the abuse is in the pressing. Ritual ethics, not chemistry, decides what a sacrament does to the soul**.

### The Draught of Vīštāspa (Yašt 9)

For King Vīštāspa, Haoma was oracles ‌and victory. In Yašt 9 the king offers the plant the sacrifice of a hundred stallions, a hundred oxen, a hundred rams, and a hundred loads of grain — and the hymn ​says Haoma grants him what armies could not buy: the most fortunate of thoughts and the most victorious of weapons, with foreknowledge of the coming war against the Turanians and their daeva-worshipping ​king Arjāsp (Yašt 9.26–30). When Vīštāspa drank the pressed haoma, his spirit was illumined and his enemies' devices laid bare; the same hymn remembers the plant's gifts of swift horses and vanquishing ‌glory. The myth dignifies strategy as piety: **the visionary draught makes foresight itself a weapon, and the patron king who drinks it fights with wisdom before he fights with armies**.

## Symbols & ‌Iconography

The iconography associated with Haoma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Haoma, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- ‌**Domain** — Sacred Plant, Immortality

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Haoma across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one ​encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Haoma carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The green stalk with golden eyes** — His Avestan self-description — the mountain ​herb that is simultaneously a god (Yašt 9.19)
- **The mortar and pestle** — The pounding-stone of the Yasna, where god, offering, and congregation meet nightly (Yasna 9–11)
- **The white haoma (parahōm)** — ‌The paradisal plant of the renovation, drunk by the resurrected that they shall not die again (Bundahišn 30)
- **Spring water and milk** — The two companions of the pressing — purity and ​nourishment joined in the consecrated draught
- **Mount Hara (Alborz)** — The cosmic axis where the first pressing happened and Mithra keeps his watch — the sacrament's original altar (Yašt 9.16; 10.13)

## ​Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Haoma with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Zoroastrian name of this ‌type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable ​forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀, sanctuary or cult remains tied to sacred plant and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed ​form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Haoma** is sacred plant, immortality. The name means "The pressed one" and belongs to the zoroastrian tradition.

### Sacred Name

The ‌restoration Haoma returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Sacred Plant

Central domain: sacred plant, immortality.

### Living Tradition

Honored in zoroastrian myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple ​despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### The First Pressing

On the heights of Hara the green, golden-eyed plant was first pressed — the primordial sacrament of the Avesta (Yašt 9.16).

### Right Pressing, Wrong ‌Pressing

Zarathuštra reproaches Haoma for the draught of the false priests; the plant answers with a roll of righteous pressers (Yasna 9.3–8).

### The Visionary Draught

For King Vīštāspa's hundredfold sacrifice, Haoma grants ​foreknowledge of the war and 'the most victorious of weapons' (Yašt 9.26).

### The Living Yasna

The nightly pounding of twigs with water and milk — performed for millennia, and still performed today ​(Yasna 9–11).

## Across Cultures

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Haoma may be likened to ​figures in neighboring traditions without being identical to them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Haoma makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

The modern afterlife of Haoma includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning ‌for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Haoma remains findable and citable.

To contemplate Haoma is to hold the idea of sacred Plant, Immortality in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "The ​pressed one" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as sacred Plant, Immortality · The pressed one.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Haoma**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source ‌tradition wrote the name in Avestan rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *haoma* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional ​spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling ‌as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **h**, ​**a**, **o**, **m**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep ‌the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

Its sphere — Sacred Plant, Immortality — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a ‌way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Haoma**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a ‌living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, ​between a tradition and a trend. **Haoma** is one such vote.
